title: A wrapper with an export line

jobs: Check the Coromandel source slip
Lay the two practice ends
Open the wrapper stand
notes: The India and Indonesia lines keep their separate roles.
The plain end markers let a reader tell an edge from the central field.

Set both plain edge markers on the trail tray
outcomes: The first reader can cite where the cloth was made and for which market. A later fold remains due.
A keeper aligns the two edge marks and clips the fabric’s written origin beside them after the opening.
revisit: Clip the export line beyond the making line
The late proof lets a reader follow both places without converting the market into a maker’s address.

object.title: Oversize Hip Wrapper (tapis)
object.medium: cotton; plain weave; drawn resist, painted mordants, dyed
object.observation: The Cleveland catalogue describes this cotton wrapper as made on India’s Coromandel Coast for export to Indonesia. It lists drawn resist and painted mordants.
object.limit: Export context concerns the cloth trade. The individual owner and complete journey are open.
object.altText: Woven wrapper with a small repeating field and dark red ends.

title: What each edge is made of
task: Eome has a keeper waiting for the catalogue terms and a handler who wants to locate the tablet-woven edge in the practice copy.
jobs: Read the three technique lines
Set the plain edge against the cuff
Open the robe stand
notes: Cotton, embroidery and tablet-woven edging have their own lines.
A peg marks the cuff edge and leaves the main practice shape free.
choices: Post the three technique lines at Fern Station
Send the cuff-and-edge rehearsal to the trail
outcomes: A reader finds the material structure from the accession before seeing the fold.
A handler moves the cuff, checks the position of the edge and later receives the material slip.
revisit: Place the edging tag beside the mock cuff
Now the proof keeps body, embroidery and edge visible as three specific features.

object.title: Woman's robe with crimson flora
object.medium: Plain weave: cotton (hand-spun, indigo dyed), embroidery: silk, cotton; tablet-woven (edges)
object.dimensions: neck edge to hem: 119.4 cm (47 in.); width across shoulders: 158.1 cm (62 1/4 in.)
object.observation: The catalogue lists indigo-dyed hand-spun cotton, silk and cotton embroidery and tablet-woven edges.
object.limit: The record describes this robe’s materials. A source credit does not identify a named weaver.
object.altText: Dark robe with red and pink embroidered flowers and detailed edges.

title: A carpet end with its own motif
task: One visitor wants the measured knot density. A handler needs to see a plain short end and the central field separately.

Lay the plain short end on the work rail
Open the carpet stand

Send the marked practice end to Listening Trail

A handler can locate the short end from their side of the rail. The maker attribution follows the check.
revisit: Hold the end tab apart from the knot range
The late proof keeps a counted area and one specific end feature separate.

object.title: Turkmen Main Carpet
object.medium: Wool, knotted pile, 128-136 symmetrical knots per square inch
object.observation: Cleveland attributes this main carpet to a Yomud weaver and records 128–136 symmetrical knots per square inch.
object.limit: Knot density is a catalogue measurement. The record leaves the precise home of this particular carpet open.
object.altText: Dark rectangular pile carpet with repeating diamond shapes and ornamental end bands.

title: An edge that complicates the central design
task: A visitor is matching designs in the centre. The maker field needs the catalogue’s border evidence too.
jobs: Read the Saryk attribution against the narrower border
Place two plain border examples in a frame
Open the shared-motif stand
notes: The border evidence and broad geography travel on the written slip.
A practice frame highlights the edge that stayed out of the general view.
choices: Lead with the qualified maker line at Fern Station
Keep the plain edge comparator on the trail
outcomes: A reader can cite the minor border and preserve both possible places.
A helper compares the centre and edge before the catalogue explanation reaches the tray.
revisit: Pin the qualified attribution beside the border aid
The shelf links two observed areas without assigning the shared centre motif to a single weaver.

object.title: Turkmen Main Carpet
object.medium: Wool, silk; 171 symmetrical (Turkish) knots per square inch
object.observation: The museum describes a Saryk carpet with triangular minor borders and a central motif shared with other weavers.
object.limit: The record leaves two possibilities for the place of making. A copied pattern supplies a comparison, not a single maker identification.
object.altText: Wide red carpet with repeating small motifs and a patterned border.

title: The embroidered square and its fringe

Open the square template to its fringe stops
Set out the shawl proof

A mock fringe stop keeps an edge visible when a viewer sees only the centre.

Leave the opened square with the trail keeper
outcomes: The first reader sees why the wool ground and silk and metal threads each matter.
The keeper puts the fringe mark next to the central outline and clips on the stitch source when it comes.
revisit: Slip the stitch proof beside the opened edge
The viewer can check an edge and later locate the source for the stitch.

object.title: Square Shawl
object.medium: Silk and silver filé, wool: chain stitch embroidery
object.dimensions: Overall including fringe: 212.1 x 212.1 cm (83 1/2 x 83 1/2 in.)
object.observation: The catalogue records wool, silk and silver filé and identifies chain stitch embroidery on this shawl.
object.limit: The stated materials and stitch come from the catalogue. The wardrobe or gathering this shawl belonged to remains open.
object.altText: Square shawl with a circular red central design and uneven fringe on two sides.

title: A bag with two kinds of fibre in its pile
task: Eome can send a note about the pile or hang a plain pocket where handling tells the difference between the front and an opening.

Hang a plain pocket with its opening marked
Open the bag display

An upright paper pocket helps a visitor find the opening.

Send a handling pocket to the Trail

A trail handler can use the pocket before the written pile note arrives.
revisit: Rehang the fibre tab beside the storage opening
The later proof shows how a bag can have a material record and a separate handling note.

object.title: Storage Bag
object.medium: Wool (warp, weft and pile), silk (pile); asymmetrically knotted pile
object.observation: The Met lists wool for warp, weft and pile, and silk in the asymmetrically knotted pile.
object.limit: The fibre list describes the bag’s construction. The contents and particular user remain open.
object.altText: Rectangular patterned storage bag on a pale background.

title: A robe’s measured back line
task: A runner keeps asking for the length around the front. The two work orders preserve where the museum measured and where a person sees the shape.

Lay an open robe shape on its practice fold
Open the ikat proof
notes: The figure stays beside the named centre-back line.
The front opens without becoming the route of the catalogue measure.

Send the practice fold to Listening Trail
outcomes: The rack shows a boundary around the measured length.
The trail reader opens the plain fold and can later connect it to the different measured line.
revisit: Move the measure tab to the actual catalogue line
Both reading paths now lead to the accession and its centre-back label.

object.title: Robe
object.medium: Silk, cotton; ikat woven
object.observation: The Met lists silk and cotton, ikat weaving and a length of 129.5 centimetres at the centre back.
object.limit: The length names a specific measured line. The catalogue leaves the maker and wearer unrecorded here.
object.altText: Robe with pointed stripes in strong colours and an open front.

title: A repeat that turns each time
task: A mounting crew needs either the actual measurement or two plain repeat arrows for people who encounter only one section.

Lay two plain repeat arrows in alternate directions
Open the long carpet stand
notes: The recorded rug length and storage-tube length stay separate.
The next example faces the opposite way to the first.

Keep the repeat arrows visible at the Trail tray
outcomes: A reader can judge how big a display needs to be without treating the tube as the work.
A handler can align successive sections. The table of rug and tube measures follows.
revisit: Set a reversing arrow on the second model panel
The additional proof shows why a repeated shape need not face the same direction.

object.title: Carpet with Palm Trees, Ibexes, and Birds
object.medium: Cotton (warp and weft), wool (pile); asymmetrically knotted pile
object.dimensions: Rug: L. 328 in. (833.1 cm) W. 108 in. (274.3 cm) Wt. 132 lbs. (59.9 kg) Storage Tube: L. 132 in. (335.3 cm) Diam. 9 in. (22.9 cm)

object.altText: Long narrow pile carpet with brown borders and repeated plant and animal shapes.

title: A panel and a longer imagined repeat
task: Eome can send a measured panel first or lay out two plain shapes that make a possible joint easier to see.

Place two plain repeat stencils on the tray
Open the chintz panel view
notes: The early slip gives the dimensions of the surviving panel.
Two mock repeats show where a continuation could go.

Bring the possible repeat joins to the Trail tray
outcomes: A reader can find the exact panel without treating it as an entire cloth.
A handler follows both mock seams and leaves the possible extension marked as an example.
revisit: Mark the surviving edge before the possible extension
The late panel marks existence and reconstruction as two different parts of the display.

object.title: Textile Panel of Chintz
object.medium: Cotton; printed
object.observation: The Met records an eighteenth-century printed cotton panel at 66 by 48.3 centimetres.
object.limit: The dimension belongs to this panel. The rest of a larger cloth remains open.
object.altText: Printed cotton panel with a dark floral pattern on a light background.

title: A cover with a second size

Send the mounting demonstration to Listening Trail

A visitor now finds the actual object dimension beside the mounting plan.

object.title: Cover (Rumal)
object.medium: Cotton; plain weave, mordant dyed and painted, resist dyed
object.observation: The Met distinguishes the cotton rumal’s size from the size of its mount and describes a mordant-and-resist dyeing process.

object.altText: Small rectangular patterned cover with a dark border and a large circular centre.

title: Two part weights, one assembled bowl

The shelf now lets readers check all three readings and preserve the role of each measured configuration.

object.title: Bowl
object.medium: Zinc alloy; cast, engraved, inlaid with silver and brass (bidri ware)

object.altText: A low dark bowl and its matching patterned cover, with reflective inlaid lines.

title: Two possible places for one painted bowl

revisit: Clip the two-place line below one observed surface
The late proof keeps the decoration claim and place alternatives on distinct lines.

object.title: Bowl with Two Birds

object.observation: The Cleveland catalogue describes two dark slip-painted birds over a light slip ground. It gives Nishapur or Samarkand as possible origins.

object.altText: Round pale bowl with two painted birds facing one another.

title: Height with a cover attached

object.title: Globular Ewer

The late proof links both pieces and keeps the lost contents line open.

object.title: Fish-Shaped Box
object.medium: Zinc alloy; cast, engraved, inlaid with silver and brass (bidri ware)

object.observation: The Met describes an inlaid bidri box with two parts and catalogues an overall length of 23.5 centimetres.
object.limit: The fish shape is in the record. The individual contents and user remain open.
object.altText: Small fish-shaped metal box with a patterned surface and visible join.

object.title: Bowl Decorated in the 'Beveled Style'

object.title: Bowl with Arabic Inscription, "Blessing, Prosperity, Well-being, Happiness"

object.dimensions: H. 4 1/4 (10.8 cm) Max Diam. 14 in. (35.6 cm)

title: The building and the making date

object.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art
